extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors querying literary agents (debut novelists, upmarket/literary fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing a one-page query letter to secure literary-agent representation for an upmarket/literary debut novel; focuses on how to structure the opening hook, plot synopsis, comps, and brief author bio. Advice is practical and aimed at getting full requests and offers of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening paragraph: title, word count, genre, comps + hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your title, word count, and genre (and comps) in the first paragraph, and open with a hook that captures the agent's attention and gives a one-sentence description of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I often advise my clients to include a hook in the opening of their letters. Not only will it hopefully capture the agent's attention from the first line, but it also helps make that first sentence flow a little more smoothly. Since it’s important to include your title, word count, genre, and comps in that first paragraph, a hook gives you an extra little opportunity to sell your book to the agent, AND you now have a way to describe your book in one sentence….” Example: the author opens with a one-line hook that includes the protagonist and the central setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comps sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide comparative titles (comps) to situate your book in the marketplace; choose comps that help an agent understand tone/audience/market fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I’ll admit, my comps sentence is not the most exciting, but it did the job. There are many more creative ways to do this, and I recommend checking out this piece we ran in Sub Club, where agents gave us the scoop on what they look for in comps.” Be mindful of which comps will resonate with a particular agent; comps don't need to be flashy, they need to be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the scene quickly and tightly; prioritize plot
rubrics_metrics.description: In the synopsis portion of the query, set scene and character quickly and focus on PLOT rather than long background or emotional exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “It’s important to set the scene as quickly and tightly as possible. The challenge here is to want to provide background information or lengthy explanations of your characters’ motivations or emotional states that trigger the opening chain of events. But this space is for PLOT. Since I found the three-act structure extremely helpful, I tried to think of how to get to the inciting incident as quickly as possible here, while telling who my character is and where the story is set.” Use three-act thinking to compress set-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the inciting incident explicit in the query so the agent sees what kicks the story into motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author flags the line in the sample as “Inciting incident!” — be explicit about what event changes the protagonist's circumstances and launches the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the point of no return / Act II transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate the moment or decision that represents the point of no return — how the protagonist is forced into Act II and cannot go back to the prior status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “The point of no return! This is how we move into Act 2 of the story. Nothing is the same. [Protagonist] can’t go back now.” Use a concise sentence to signal escalation and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle: focus on cause-effect; avoid too many side plots or characters
rubrics_metrics.description: In the middle-summary, avoid listing multiple side characters, subplots, or emotional detail that will make the synopsis feel chaotic; instead, show how each scene/revelation leads to the next (domino effect) and maintain the main through-thread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “...by adding in more character names and plot lines here, in such a small space, it could make my story sound chaotic and unorganized. Or it's just information we don’t need to know when summarizing the story. Take out emotionality, side plots, and extra characters and focus on how each scene is a reaction to another. One domino tipping over the next. Since I opened my letter with a line about Rita’s mother, I need to keep that thread throughout... even though it’s not the only relationship in the story.”

rubrics_metrics.name: End the synopsis with a cliffhanger / stakes-driven climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Close the plot summary by showing the climax or a cliffhanger that demonstrates stakes and leaves the agent wanting more (indicating there is more of the story to read in the manuscript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “It’s important to both show the agent you have more of your story coming (with reactions to all the dominoes you have just lined up) AND leave them dying to know more. My hope here was for the agent to want to read the manuscript so they could find out just how badly Rita screws up and that money and power are key themes that influence the plot.” Aim to balance showing resolution and withholding enough to entice a full request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention relevant experience/authority briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have relevant real-world experience related to your book’s subject matter, include a concise line noting it to establish authority and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I felt it was important to note this because of my extensive experience. Ten years is worth a mention, and it most likely shows why I wanted to write this novel. Not that you ever need to justify WHY you want to write about something, but I thought that by adding it, the agent would understand that I have a firm grasp on a landscape that we don’t see discussed in novels very often. It gave me authority.” Keep it short and directly relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise author bio; prior publication not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a short bio with relevant roles/publications but understand that lacking prior publications is usually not fatal; let the manuscript speak for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample bio lists editorial roles, newsletter, podcast, residence, and next project. The author notes: “Notice how your girl has NO PRIOR PUBLICATIONS... I even asked Jenny, my agent, about it... she basically said she didn’t care lol … But if you are like me and querying without prior publication, know that it most likely won’t hinder you. Your current novel will speak for itself.” Keep bios compact and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and accurate with genre labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Label your book in a way that reflects its market placement but be prepared to swap or adjust labels (literary, upmarket, book-club fiction) depending on agent feedback or interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I sent this query as both literary and upmarket. I made the swap when it looked like an agent was more interested in one genre over the other. They are both similar enough that I felt I was able to do this without a problem. I also tried ‘book club fiction.’ In the end, the agent that I signed with said it was upmarket, and that is what we used when going out on submission, too.” Accuracy and flexibility both matter.
